question: In the 2015 Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibition titled after the Chinese zodiac animal of 2015, how many of the "twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac" have a hand visible?

history.name: user
history.content: In the 2015 Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibition titled after the Chinese zodiac animal of 2015, how many of the "twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac" have a hand visible?

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Task: Determine the count of zodiac figures with a visible hand in the Met’s 2015 exhibition named after the zodiac animal of that year (Year of the Sheep/Ram). Plan: 1) Identify the Met’s official 2015 exhibition page (likely "Celebration of the Year of the Ram"). 2) Find the related object/set for the twelve zodiac animals displayed/linked in the same gallery context. 3) From the official object/exhibition materials (image and description), establish which animals show a visible hand and count them. WebSurfer, please locate the official Met page(s) and any object page for the twelve zodiac animals associated with Gallery 207 in 2015.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content: Search done for: Met 2015 Year of the Ram Gallery 207 twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac. Top results: 1) Celebration of the Year of the Ram — The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Jan 17–Apr 19, 2015), Weber Galleries, Gallery 207. URL: https://www.metmuseum.org/exhibitions/listings/2015/year-of-the-ram 2) Twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac — The Met Collection (Qing dynasty jade set), on view in Gallery 207. URL: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/42102. These appear directly relevant and contemporaneous with the 2015 display context.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Open the jade set page for the twelve animals and extract any description that mentions hands/poses, plus confirm if this object was on view in Gallery 207. If possible, capture the large image link for closer inspection.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content: Opened: Twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac (object 42102). Page states: "On view at The Met Fifth Avenue in Gallery 207." Description includes: "Qing-dynasty master carvers individualized each animal... The snake, for example, sits calmly with his hands in long, loose sleeves." This implies the snake’s hands are not visible. The page provides a high-res image via IIIF: https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/api/collection/v1/iiif/42102/154217/main-image. This set appears connected to the gallery context of the 2015 Year of the Ram exhibition location (Gallery 207).

history.name: FileSurfer
history.content: Attempted to parse the Assistant’s JSON, but it is invalid: single quotes used for keys/strings, a missing closing brace on the Rooster object line, trailing comma after the last array element, and a non-boolean value ('unknown') for hand_visible. I performed a best-effort fallback by scanning for the literal token pattern hand_visible: true. I detected 10 occurrences. The lines for Snake and Rooster were not machine-decodable as boolean true (Snake has 'unknown'; Rooster has 'ture' and a missing brace). Passing count=10 to the orchestrator with low confidence.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Synthesis: The object page confirms the snake’s hands are within long sleeves (suggesting not visible). The Assistant’s structured data failed to parse, and FileSurfer’s fallback count detected 10 explicit "hand_visible: true" entries; the two problematic entries were Snake (unknown/likely not visible) and Rooster (malformed line, not counted). Given the Gallery 207 alignment with the 2015 Year of the Ram display context, we’ll proceed with the conservative parsed count. Provisional answer: 10 animals have a visible hand.

mistake_reason: At step 5, the Assistant produced a malformed structured output intended for parsing: it used single quotes instead of double quotes, contained a missing closing brace for the Rooster item, included a trailing comma in the array, and assigned a string ('unknown') instead of a boolean. It also wrapped the JSON with conversational text ("Here’s the JSON:"), violating the strict schema. This FM-4.4 formatting error prevented downstream parsing, forcing a lossy fallback that undercounted visible-hand entries and led to the wrong final answer.
